claim_results.english_source_claim: In this historic judgment, the Supreme Court established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' of the Indian Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331].
claim_results.tamil_claim: இந்த வரலாற்றுச் சிறப்புமிக்க தீர்ப்பில், உச்ச நீதிமன்றம் இந்திய அரசியலமைப்பின் 'அடிப்படை கட்டமைப்புக் கோட்பாட்டை' (Basic Structure Doctrine) உருவாக்கியது [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331].

claim_results.english_source_claim: The Court decided that while Parliament has wide power under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, it cannot use this power to alter, destroy, or remove the basic framework or core features of the Constitution, such as democracy, secularism, and judicial review [Page 128] [Page 331] [Page 369].
claim_results.tamil_claim: அடிப்படை உரிமைகள் உட்பட அரசியலமைப்பின் எந்தவொரு விதியையும் திருத்த பிரிவு 368-ன் கீழ் நாடாளுமன்றத்திற்கு பரந்த அதிகாரம் இருந்தாலும், ஜனநாயகம், மதச்சார்பின்மை மற்றும் நீதிமன்ற ஆய்வு போன்ற அரசியலமைப்பின் அடிப்படை வடிவமைப்பு அல்லது முக்கிய அம்சங்களை மாற்றவோ, அழிக்கவோ அல்லது நீக்கவோ இந்த அதிகாரத்தைப் பயன்படுத்த முடியாது என்று நீதிமன்றம் முடிவு செய்தது [Page 128] [Page 331] [Page 369].

claim_results.english_source_claim: Parliament can pass amendments to give effect to directive principles, but it cannot completely cut off the courts' power of judicial review to verify if a law actually serves those public purposes [Page 369] [Page 502].
claim_results.tamil_claim: வழிகாட்டு நெறிமுறைகளை அமல்படுத்துவதற்கு நாடாளுமன்றம் திருத்தங்களை நிறைவேற்றலாம், ஆனால் ஒரு சட்டம் உண்மையில் அந்த பொது நோக்கங்களுக்குப் பயன்படுகிறதா என்பதைச் சரிபார்க்கும் நீதிமன்றங்களின் நீதித்துறை ஆய்வு அதிகாரத்தை முழுமையாகப் பறிக்க முடியாது [Page 369] [Page 502].

supporting_source_context.case_overview: Writ Petition (Civil) 135 of 1970 was filed by His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, challenging the constitutional validity of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, Parliament enacted the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 [Page 1] [Page 477]. A special Bench of 13 Judges was constituted to determine the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, the correctness of the majority decision in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, and the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments [Page 1] [Page 71] [Page 375] [Page 426] [Page 470].
supporting_source_context.court_reasoning:
The Court evaluated the scope of Article 368 and overruled the majority view in Golak Nath case, holding that Article 368 contains both the power and procedure for amending the Constitution and that the word 'law' in Article 13(2) applies only to ordinary legislation, not to constitutional amendments made in exercise of constituent power [Page 7] [Page 115] [Page 147] [Page 153] [Page 204] [Page 375] [Page 451].

On the extent of the amending power, a majority of the Bench held that Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter, destroy, or emasculate the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331]. Judges including Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Jaganmohan Reddy, and Khanna JJ. held that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution including fundamental rights, it cannot alter the basic features or essential elements of the Constitution [Page 71] [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331]. Khanna J. reasoned that the word 'amendment' postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of its identity or basic structure [Page 331].

Regarding Section 2 of the 25th Amendment, the Court held that replacing 'compensation' with 'amount' in Article 31(2) is valid and that courts cannot review the adequacy of the amount fixed or determined, provided the amount is not completely illusory or arbitrary [Page 58] [Page 134] [Page 147] [Page 420] [Page 464].

Regarding Section 3 of the 25th Amendment (Article 31C), Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, and Jaganmohan Reddy JJ. held Article 31C invalid in whole or part due to delegation of constituent power and abrogation of fundamental rights [Page 64] [Page 109] [Page 141] [Page 255]. Khanna J. sustained the main provision of Article 31C but struck down the second part containing the declaration clause ('and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court...'), holding that excluding judicial review strikes at the basic structure of the Constitution [Page 369]. Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, and Chandrachud JJ. found no implied limitations on Article 368 and upheld all the challenged amendments in full [Page 179] [Page 204] [Page 286] [Page 426] [Page 458] [Page 502].
supporting_source_context.decision_or_conclusion:
The Supreme Court delivered its decision with the following main conclusions:
1. The majority view in Golak Nath's case is wrong; the power to amend the Constitution is located in Article 368, and 'law' in Article 13(2) does not include a constitutional amendment [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 375].
2. The Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 58] [Page 128] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 426] [Page 486].
3. Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter or destroy the basic structure or framework of the Constitution [Page 128] [Page 236] [Page 331].
4. Section 2 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 is valid [Page 58] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 242] [Page 426].
5. The first part of Article 31C (introduced by Section 3 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment) is valid subject to judicial review regarding whether a law has a direct and reasonable nexus with Article 39(b) or (c); the second part of Article 31C (the declaration clause excluding judicial review) is unconstitutional and void [Page 141] [Page 255] [Page 369] [Page 502].
6. The Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is valid [Page 71] [Page 147] [Page 204] [Page 426] [Page 502].
7. The writ petitions were remitted to the Constitution Bench to be determined in accordance with the judgment and the law [Page 71] [Page 502] [Page 2264].
